clue.text: Bar teller of falsehoods that's taken aback

indicators.note: Somebody taken aback is knocked backwards, so the word just named is written out from its far end.

parts.note: a teller of falsehoods is a liar, and that is the word to be turned

explanation.surface: Shutting the door on a known liar, who is startled to find himself refused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' opens the clue as a verb — refuse someone entry — and is wanted as the noun. The word that turns round names the person, not the act of keeping him out.
explanation.definitionFit: A rail is the bar running along a fence, a banister or a coat rack: a straight length of wood or metal fixed in place.

clue.text: Phone program allowed right phone network: this'll bear fruit

definitions.note: The setter defines by describing what the thing does rather than naming it, so a whole sentence stands where the answer is a noun.

parts.note: an app is the little program you download onto a handset
to let is to allow
r is the standard short form of right
EE is one of Britain's mobile networks, initials of Everything Everywhere

explanation.surface: A mobile app cleared to use the right network, with promising things to come.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Phone' does two separate jobs and neither is horticultural: once for the app, once for EE, the British network formed out of Orange and T-Mobile. The colon is the setter's join.
explanation.definitionFit: An apple tree is a thing that literally bears fruit, so the definition names it by its job instead of calling it a tree at all.

clue.text: Not gramme; not 'timeless' litre — flipping imperial unit!

indicators.note: Something timeless has no time in it, so the letter that stands for time drops out of the word beside it.
To flip a thing is to turn it over, so everything gathered so far is written out starting from the other end.

parts.note: the little word itself, taken as it stands
g is the short form of gramme on every kitchen scale
the same word again, this time with t for time struck out of it
l is the standard abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated, rejecting one metric measure after another.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'timeless' are the setter flagging a word that carries an instruction rather than a meaning. Everything collected arrives backwards, which is why the litre's letter opens the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A long ton is the British imperial ton of 2,240 pounds, the weight the metric tonne was brought in to replace.

clue.text: In the auditorium, young lady composed

indicators.note: An auditorium is where you go to listen, so the words are worth their sound and not their spelling.

parts.note: a young lady in service is a maid, and said aloud that is what you hear

explanation.surface: A young woman keeping her poise in front of a theatre audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' reads in the surface as calm and collected; the sense wanted is put together out of parts. Maid for a young woman is archaic but alive in 'maiden' and 'old maid'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something composed has been put together — composed of brick, composed of parts — and that is the sense that swaps in, not the unruffled one.

clue.text: Fictional schoolgirl, bullied until protected by both parents

indicators.note: Whoever is protected has the others standing round them, so the letters spelt out first end up inside the pair named next.

parts.note: ma and da, the two of them, and they part to make room between
til is the short spelling of until, the one that usually wears an apostrophe
she is bullied right through the book, so the word paints the picture and gives up no letters

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl tormented at school until her mother and father step in.
explanation.walkthrough: The kind parents are the joke: in Roald Dahl's novel the Wormwoods are the last people who would protect her. 'Da' for father is Irish and northern English.
explanation.definitionFit: Matilda Wormwood is the tiny book-devouring schoolgirl of Dahl's novel, up against the headmistress Miss Trunchbull.

clue.text: Dork departs with little book

parts.note: d is what a railway timetable prints for departs
wee is Scots and northern English for little
b is the standard short form of book

explanation.surface: A nerd heading off with a slim volume under his arm.
explanation.walkthrough: Three short conventions stacked in clue order, which is only quick once you stop reading 'departs' as the sentence's verb. Wee turns up constantly and is worth owning.
explanation.definitionFit: A dweeb is American playground slang for the same boring, socially hopeless figure that dork names.

clue.text: One loves rest and recuperation, conserving energy after fuss

definitions.note: The setter writes 'One loves' where the answer is a noun; read it as 'one who loves', the person the phrase is describing.

indicators.note: To conserve something is to keep it safely inside, so the letter named next is held within the letters just found.

parts.note: ado is fuss, as in much ado about nothing

indicators.note: What comes after a thing follows behind it, so the fuss is written down first and the rest of the wordplay trails it.

parts.note: R and R is the forces' phrase for leave, written as the two letters
e is the standard abbreviation for energy

explanation.surface: Someone devoted to time off, saving their strength until the fuss dies down.
explanation.walkthrough: R and R is a military term for rest and recuperation, and the clue spells it out in full rather than trusting the abbreviation. 'One loves' is shorthand for the person who does it.
explanation.definitionFit: An adorer is the one doing the adoring — a devoted admirer, a worshipper — so 'one who loves' is the whole of the job.

clue.text: Cling together — force asunder

definitions.meaning: the old sense of holding fast to a person or a cause, the one kept in the marriage service
the butcher's sense, splitting a carcass with one heavy blade

explanation.surface: Two people holding on to each other and being pulled apart.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the classic contronym: one verb carrying two meanings that are each other's opposite, because two different Old English words fell together in modern spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: To cleave to something is to cling to it; to cleave something is to split it in two with a blow — the same six letters, opposite instructions.

clue.text: How Galileo's experiments began — misjudged act

definitions.meaning: he let weights go from a height and timed their fall, so every test started by letting go
the idiom out of ball games for the blunder that lets everybody down

explanation.surface: Galileo at the top of the tower, making a hash of his very first experiment.
explanation.walkthrough: Galileo is said to have dropped weights from the leaning tower at Pisa to show that they fall at the same rate. The idiom is American, out of baseball and football.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves are the same three words: the experiments literally began by letting a ball go, and to drop the ball is to fumble what you were trusted with.

clue.text: Finished? Let me past!

definitions.meaning: a chore dealt with is a chore no longer standing in front of you
what you shout at somebody blocking a doorway

explanation.surface: An impatient person asking whether you are done and demanding room to get by.
explanation.walkthrough: Both readings are about where a thing stands rather than what it is: a job behind you and a body in a corridor take the same four words. The question mark is the seam.
explanation.definitionFit: A finished task is out of the way, and 'out of the way!' is the shout at whoever blocks your path — one about time, one about space.

clue.text: Stadia I race around somewhere alongside Italy

indicators.note: To move around is to move with no fixed direction, so the letters before it end up anywhere but in the order given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.surface: A runner listing the stadiums on the circuit he competes around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race around' reads as an athlete's circuit, which is exactly what hides the shuffle in plain sight. Stadia is the Latin plural of stadium, and the count comes to eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: The Adriatic Sea is the long arm of the Mediterranean running the whole length of Italy's eastern coast, with Croatia on the far shore.

clue.text: Concerning bone-shaped biscuit? Turn back!

parts.note: re means concerning, the word at the head of a memo
the thing you give a dog, sold moulded into bone shapes

explanation.surface: A note about the dog biscuits that ends by ordering a turnaround.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn back!' is the definition and reads like an instruction to reverse something, which is the false trail here. The question mark marks the example: not every dog treat is bone-shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: To retreat is to turn back and go the way you came, whether from a battle or from a bad idea.

clue.text: Latin peninsula, land on the Atlantic

parts.note: l is the standard short form of Latin
Iberia is the peninsula Spain and Portugal share

explanation.surface: A stretch of the Latin world jutting out into the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: Iberia genuinely is Latin land on the Atlantic, so surface and definition both pull towards Europe; the country wanted is in West Africa. It was founded in 1822 as a home for freed American slaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberia sits on the West African coast with the Atlantic along the whole of its southern edge.

clue.text: And reefer liberated in public votes

indicators.note: Letters that have been liberated are out of their cells and free to stand anywhere, so the ones before the word are reordered.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters, and the first word is part of it

explanation.surface: The public voting to set cannabis free.
explanation.walkthrough: A reefer is a hand-rolled cannabis cigarette, and legalisation settled at the ballot box reads like a news headline. Referenda is the Latin plural; referendums is equally correct.
explanation.definitionFit: Referenda are the votes put to a whole electorate on one question, as opposed to an election that chooses people.

clue.text: Quiet Everyman hiding a sense of remorse

indicators.note: What is hidden is tucked inside something else, so the letter named next goes in among the ones already found.

parts.note: sh is the noise you make telling somebody to be quiet
the setter signs himself Everyman, so he is me
the single letter, lifted from the clue as it stands

explanation.surface: The setter quietly keeping his regrets to himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman is the setter's own signature, dropped into his puzzles most weeks, and read as 'me' it supplies two letters. The 'a' works twice over, once in the surface's phrase and once as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Shame is the feeling that you have done wrong and wish you had not — remorse as something felt rather than expressed.

clue.text: Observer — that offers weekly journalism

definitions.meaning: one who observes: somebody watching rather than taking part
the London magazine of politics and the arts that appears every Wednesday

explanation.surface: The Sunday paper this puzzle runs in, described by the journalism it prints.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics mark a title, and the Observer is the very paper carrying this crossword — misdirection and in-joke at once. The weekly wanted is a magazine, founded in 1828 and still going.
explanation.definitionFit: An observer is a spectator, one who looks on; and The Spectator is the weekly magazine, the oldest still in print.

clue.text: Brownish hue seen in Loch Restil

indicators.note: What is seen in something is already sitting there to be looked at, so the letters run unbroken through the words that follow.

parts.note: five letters in a row starting at the second, carrying on across the gap between the words

explanation.surface: A walker noticing the colour of the water in a Highland loch.
explanation.walkthrough: Loch Restil is a small loch in Argyll, below the pass called the Rest and Be Thankful, and it is there to make the line read as scenery. Hidden words love proper nouns, which nobody reads letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is the yellow-brown earth pigment, one of the oldest paints there is and the colour of cave walls.

clue.text: Tankers: they work hard with time to spare

indicators.note: Having something to spare means it is surplus to requirements, so the letter named just before is left out.

parts.note: people who work hard are toilers, from toil
t is the standard abbreviation for time, and it is the letter that goes

explanation.surface: Hard workers who still manage to finish ahead of the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With time to spare' is one idiom on the surface and has to be read in pieces: the time is a letter, and 'to spare' is the instruction to drop it. Toil is the old word for grinding labour.
explanation.definitionFit: An oiler is a tanker — the ship that carries oil, and in naval use the one that refuels the rest of the fleet at sea.

clue.text: Vehicle exercises Bond in finale — in other words, M, you only live once …

parts.note: a car is the everyday vehicle
PE is physical education, the exercise lesson at school

indicators.note: A finale is the closing number, so only the letter standing at the end of the word before it is wanted.

parts.note: the letter at the end of Bond, taken on its own
i.e. is the Latin id est, used to mean in other words
the letter as printed, lifted straight out of the clue

explanation.surface: Bond's car put through its paces in the closing scene while M has the last word.
explanation.walkthrough: M runs the Secret Service in the films, which is what makes a single letter look like a person. 'You only live once' is one life short of the Bond title everybody expects.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpe diem is Horace's 'seize the day', the tag for making the most of the time you have — which is what 'you only live once' urges.

clue.text: A tiny bit of a soupçon?

definitions.text: A tiny bit of a soupçon?

parts.note: the surface offers a quantity, the merest trace of something
read the word as it is printed and its c wears a little tail, which is a tiny bit of it in the other sense

explanation.surface: Asking for the merest trace of an amount that is already tiny.
explanation.walkthrough: Soupçon is French for a hint or a suspicion, borrowed whole into English menus. Taken as ink rather than as meaning, the printed word carries the very thing being asked for.
explanation.definitionFit: A cedilla is the hook written under a c to soften it to an s, so it is literally the smallest part of the printed word soupçon.

clue.text: Drink offered by Frenchman: his is most odd

parts.note: rum is the cane spirit, the old navy ration
m is monsieur, the French for mister
the Frenchman's own word for 'is' is est, as in c'est

explanation.surface: A drink handed over by a Frenchman whose own is stranger still.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His is' has to be split in two: the possessive belongs to the story, while the 'is' is the word the Frenchman would say. Rum meaning odd is old British slang — a rum do, a rum lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is British slang for odd or peculiar, so the superlative is the oddest of the lot.

clue.text: Breakfast's sublime bananas with no hint of bacon

indicators.note: To go bananas is to go wildly out of control, and letters out of control are letters out of their order.
A hint of something is the barest start of it, so only the opening letter of the word after it is in play.

parts.note: the seven letters that go into the shuffle before one is taken away

indicators.note: 'With no' rules the next thing out, so the letter it names never joins the others.

parts.note: the letter at the front of bacon, and the one that has to go

explanation.surface: A breakfast of glorious bananas with not a rasher of bacon in sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' is fruit on the breakfast table and a shuffle in the wordplay, and it is doing the second job. A hint of a word means its first letter — shorthand worth owning.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is one breakfast among many — the Swiss bowl of raw oats, nuts and dried fruit — so the definition names the category it belongs to.

clue.text: … terrible downfall — not fine — the only way is up

definitions.note: The setter defines by describing where the answer leaves you standing, so a whole clause does the work of a noun.

indicators.note: Something terrible is in a dreadful state, and letters in a dreadful state are no longer in their proper order.
'Not' strikes out whatever follows it, so the letter named there is left out of the shuffle.

parts.note: the eight letters that go into the shuffle before one is struck out
f is the standard short form of fine, the grade stamped on a pencil

explanation.surface: A ruinous fall from grace, with the consolation that things can only improve.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on from 16 across, so the opening dots are punctuation rather than an instruction. The dashes fence 'not fine' off as its own small order, easy to miss inside the story of the fall.
explanation.definitionFit: A lowland is the low-lying ground at the bottom of a landscape, so from it every direction out is a climb.

clue.text: Athletic Titan; legendarily achy shoulders, primarily?

definitions.text: Athletic Titan; legendarily achy shoulders, primarily?

indicators.note: What comes primarily comes first of all, so each word gives up nothing but the letter standing at its head.

parts.note: the leading letters of five words in a row, read in the order they stand

explanation.surface: A strongman of legend complaining that his shoulders are sore.
explanation.walkthrough: The Titan of the myth was sentenced to hold up the sky for ever, which is why the shoulders ache and why the sentence doubles as its own definition. The book of maps takes his name from an old frontispiece.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines: the Titan of the legend, built for the job, carrying the weight of the heavens on his shoulders.

clue.text: Artist showing some characters in laundromat is sensation

indicators.note: Characters are letters as well as people, and 'some' asks for a stretch of them rather than all, so part of what follows is on show.

parts.note: seven letters in a row, beginning inside the first word and finishing inside the last

explanation.surface: An artist exhibiting portraits in a launderette, to everyone's astonishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' is the pivot: people in the pictures on the surface, letters on the page in the wordplay. Laundromat is the American word — a launderette over here — and is there for its spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse led the Fauves and is one of the handful of painters a clue can call simply 'artist'.

clue.text: Messrs Orbison, Yankovic, Green and Bacharach heard with David by Latitude concert venue

indicators.note: Messrs is the plural of Mr, so the surnames after it stand for the men themselves and it is their first names that are wanted.

parts.note: Roy Orbison, the American singer of Oh, Pretty Woman
'Weird Al' Yankovic, the American writer of pop parodies
Al Green, the soul singer

indicators.note: What is heard is taken by its sound, so the name before it is written down as it sounds rather than as its owner spells it.

parts.note: Burt Bacharach wrote the tunes for a shelf of standards, and his forename said aloud is spelt the other way
Hal David wrote the words to Bacharach's tunes, so the two names travel together
l is the short form of latitude on a chart, and Latitude is also a music festival

explanation.surface: A bill of singers and songwriters lined up to play a summer festival.
explanation.walkthrough: Bacharach and David were the partnership behind Walk On By, which is why the names sit side by side. Latitude is the Suffolk music festival, and only the one forename is wanted for its sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Albert Hall is the domed Victorian concert hall in Kensington, the home of the Proms.

clue.text: Scotswoman is regularly bleak

parts.note: the word as printed, taken whole

indicators.note: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed interval, so every second one of the word after it is picked out and the rest dropped.

parts.note: the second and fourth letters, picked off at every other step

explanation.surface: A Scottish woman described as being consistently gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: The innocent word is 'is': tiny joining words are exactly where setters hide letters. The name is said EYE-la and comes from Islay, the Hebridean island of the peaty whiskies.
explanation.definitionFit: Isla is a Scottish forename taken from the island of Islay, so it names a Scotswoman by example rather than by description.

clue.text: Rent in North almost insane

indicators.note: Almost a word is not quite the whole of it, so the last letter never arrives.
Somebody insane is out of their right mind, and these letters are out of their right order.

parts.note: north stopped just short of its end: four of the five letters

explanation.surface: Rents in the north of the country reaching barely believable levels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' is money on the surface and the past participle of rend in the answer — cloth rent in two. Reading the line as a grumble about housing is what stops you seeing the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something torn is rent: the old past participle of rend, still used of cloth and of a country split in two.
